changelog.summary: Scaffold and content model: six layers, thirteen frameworks, six sources, six functions, eight canonical pillars with two views, 48 matrix cells, four doors, six helpers, the AI column.

Owner's rulings and the G1 gauntlet fixes; authored verification status; twelve matrix cells re-authored from primaries; a seven-step civilian door with a verification step; SP 1800-35 and OMB M-25-21 added as sources; contractor landings on the other door; capability ids on the {{dow}} view.
Labels, description and about text the web wrapper renders; no change to the stack's facts.

Solutions as a new entity kind, with DISA Thunderdome and Navy Flank Speed measured against the {{dow}} zero trust activities; the zero trust portfolio office named; the zero trust baseline for operational technology added at layer 3 with a door step and a helper answer; a helper answer on where solutions land; the {{dow}} door's first step describes component implementation plans; CORA described as a readiness assessment and the verbs at layer 5 distinguished.

Labels for the static web page; plain-reader fixes from the G2 gauntlet: abbreviations spelled out at first use in each door, a plain definition of zero trust, a note on the department's two names, a key to the verification labels, and the activity counts behind Target and Advanced Level. No change to the stack's facts.

A glossary of every abbreviation the app uses, each expansion checked against its publisher, plus a definition of Community Profile; rechecks of CMMC Phase 2, DTM 25-003, SP 1353 and IR 8596; the CORA wording ruling recorded; the congressional statement cited with its address and authors; helper answers name the joint standard ISO/IEC 27001.

The web wrapper renders the glossary as its own section, spells out each abbreviation at its first use in every section with a glossary popover when scripts run, gives phones a labeled section menu that names the section in view, labels matrix cells with their pillar on narrow screens, and prints the department's view in under 20 pages with every other section complete; the door for everyone else defines federal contract information and controlled unclassified information where a reader sorts by them.

Licenses named: the text under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International and the code under the MIT License, with a licensing paragraph in About and glossary entries for both licenses; the text of the privacy policy and the support page published beside the app; four glossary lines and one verification note reworded so no private publisher's wording is copied. No change to the stack's facts.

Labels and text for the new look of the web page: the front door's line, buttons and door meta lines, a footer with the licenses and three links, and a sentence on how the app was built; the typefaces, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono, named with their license, the SIL Open Font License 1.1, with glossary entries for IBM, SIL and OFL; the privacy policy names the source repository among the outside links; the About paragraph opens with the README's wording. No change to the stack's facts.

Licensing: from this version, Lensatic's code and its own text are all rights reserved. Earlier versions were released under the MIT License and CC BY 4.0, and those grants still apply to copies of them. The typefaces stay under the SIL Open Font License.
Why the name: a short explanation of the lensatic compass in About, linked from the front door, with the maker's photo. AI is treated as a well-known term and no longer spelled out.

Wording for the iOS app: the support page says the app is built from the same content, the privacy policy says the app keeps nothing, and the introductions to the doors, the stack and the matrix have app versions that describe the app's screens. No change to the stack's facts.

Link previews now use the Lensatic pitch; the short line and the wayfinder line are stored with the content for the README, the repository and the store listing. The start screen of the iPhone app gains its title.

The content the iOS app ships with. Corrections and updates from the pre-release review: the defense contractor door names the SPRS assessment score and cyber incident reporting, and names its DFARS clause in its first step; the CMMC entry says it binds contractors handling FCI or CUI; the doors give the clause number used under the FAR overhaul, and the SP 800-171 entry notes the proposed rule that would require Revision 3; the Everyone else door says when a contract can bind you and names the CIS Controls as a smaller catalog; the zero trust for OT entry says the document sets no deadline and records the dates the department has announced but not printed; the CISA maturity model links to CISA's current page and says how it binds; the FedRAMP answer describes both its Rev5 and 20x paths; the EO 14028 note says how National Security Systems are covered; the CMMC news release carries its printed headline; four matrix cells, two Respond cells and the Identify and Recover cards say more precisely what to do; the AI column says where AI lands in the matrix and counts three frameworks and a quick-start guide; the OT and ISO answers point to CISA's OT guidance and to NIST's cross-map; the glossary reads true in the app as well as on the page, names both FISMA acts, and adds SPRS and S. (Senate); the stack legend and the Sources heading describe the dashed chips as they are; MITRE ATT&CK is named in full where it first appears; the front door's date is labeled as the latest source check; the typefaces are IBM's own files, with IBM's license notice; and small corrections to citations, editions and source notes, with the dates of the sources checked again.

The AI column adds Zero Trust for AI Systems, Version 1.0 of 4 September 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI), an OASIS Open Project. The column note gains a sentence on where the paper keeps authorization and now counts four frameworks; the glossary adds CoSAI and OASIS Open.

The RMF entry now notes the Cybersecurity Risk Management Construct that the {{dow}} CIO announced in September 2025 and presents as the successor to the RMF process, and the glossary adds CSRMC. The {{dow}} door's first step says what to do about the implementation plan now and names the expired memorandum; its steps add the roadmap's courses of action and the yearly waiver. The Thunderdome note dates DISA's release 28 July 2023 and its republication 2 August 2023, and names DISA's own copy as the one read. The CMMC entry's two layers are rechecked, with the next check on 10 November 2026, and the SP 1353 entry records a recheck.
The doors are now trailheads, to match the compass and map language, and the version line's link reads Why 'Lensatic'?
About now opens with the wayfinder line: what Lensatic is, and what it is not.
The front no longer leads with the offline line, and Lensatic no longer calls itself offline; About keeps no account and no data collected.
AI is no longer a glossary link across the page; it links to its definition only in the AI column.

meta.description: An explainer of the United States federal cybersecurity framework stack: what each framework is for, how the frameworks relate, who each one binds, and where zero trust and AI land.
meta.tagline: Federal cyber frameworks are thick woods. Lensatic is the compass.
meta.pitch: Federal cyber frameworks are thick woods. Lensatic is the compass: find where you stand, see which framework applies, and take a bearing on your next waypoint.
meta.wayfinder: Lensatic is a wayfinder, not a crosswalk. It guides you, showing which framework answers which question and how the trails converge, so you know your bearing before you step into a control catalog or navigate the cyber assurance terrain.

nameStory: A lensatic compass is the Army's field compass. You sight a landmark through its lens, read the bearing off the dial, and move out knowing which way you're headed. Lensatic does the same for the framework stack: find where you stand, see which framework applies, and take a bearing on what comes next.
The maker learned land navigation with one and has kept it for more than 20 years.

dow.renderRule: Prose renders the department only from this object, through render tokens: the token dow alone renders the abbreviation, the token dow.current renders the current name, and a first mention renders the current name followed by the abbreviation in parentheses. dow.statusNote: The statutory title remains Department of Defense pending Congress. On 9 September 2026, 10 U.S.C. 111 still read Department of Defense (text current through 8 September 2026); the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act, enacted 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60, did not change it; the FY2027 bill the House of Representatives passed on 22 July 2026 as H.R. 8800 carries a section deeming statutory references to the Department of Defense to be references to the department's current name, and the Senate bill (S. 4784) carries a section redesignating the department in titles 10, 32 and 37; neither is law.

ztPfmo.name: Zero Trust Portfolio Management Office
ztPfmo.established: January 2022, within the {{dow}} CIO's office; Directive-type Memorandum (DTM) 25-003 of 17 July 2025 set out its role in an issuance.
ztPfmo.role: Coordinates, synchronizes and accelerates zero trust adoption across the {{dow}} enterprise. DTM 25-003, whose printed expiry of 17 July 2026 has passed with no successor instruction found, directs components to submit their zero trust implementation plans each year to the CIO through the office and to U.S. Cyber Command through its Cyber Defense Command, and gives the office's Chief Zero Trust Officer their review and approval. The office conducted the 2023 purple team assessment of the Navy's Flank Speed and sponsored the 2024 round.

verification.note: Current name read on 16 September 2026 in the CIO's operational technology guidance, cleared 18 November 2025, which names the office and gives its purpose, and in NSA's January 2026 implementation guideline primer. The office has no page of its own on dowcio.war.gov; its documents are listed in the CIO library (https://dowcio.war.gov/Library/). January 2022 is printed in the DoD Zero Trust Strategy (https://dowcio.war.gov/Portals/0/Documents/Library/DoD-ZTStrategy.pdf). DTM 25-003 (https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dtm/DTM%2025-003.PDF), incorporating change 1 of 2 September 2025, establishes the office in an issuance, directs component heads to submit implementation plans annually to the CIO through it (Attachment 2, paragraph 11.d; the Military Departments are components under its applicability) and gives the Chief Zero Trust Officer the review and approval of those plans (Attachment 3, paragraph 5.a.(2)); the DTM's printed expiry of 17 July 2026 has passed and the issuance library still lists it. The Department of the Navy CIO reports that the office conducted the summer 2023 purple team assessment of Flank Speed against the 91 Target activities and sponsored the spring 2024 round against all 152 (https://www.doncio.navy.mil/ContentView.aspx?ID=18012); no publisher page names the office as the tester of any other solution. DTM 25-003 rechecked on 17 September 2026: still listed with change 1; no later change, extension or successor instruction.

verification.note: NIST CSWP 29 PDF fetched: title, version 2.0 and 26 February 2024 match. authority.note: Voluntary by design for everyone outside the executive branch; every federal agency head, civilian and {{dow}}, is directed to use it by Executive Order 13800, as the communication layer above the mandatory RMF and SP 800-53.

verification.note: Section 1 of the document: the CSF 'may be adopted voluntarily and through governmental policies and mandates'. The activity chart prints Version OT.1.3 as of 25 September 2025 and counts 84 Target, 21 Advanced and 105 total activities under the User, Device, Application & Workload, Data, Network & Environment, Automation & Orchestration and Visibility & Analytics pillars. doors.title: Everyone else

doors.paragraph: Nothing on this stack binds you by its own force; a government contract can, and the two cases below say how. If a customer or regulator names a framework, start from that one and work up and down the stack from there. Verification is whoever checks your evidence: an internal audit, a certifier, or a customer assessment; the layer 5 entries here are federal. helper.question: Is CSF 2.0 mandatory?
helper.answer: Not by its own force. CSF 2.0 is voluntary by design, and Executive Order 13800 makes each federal agency head, civilian and {{dow}}, use it. For federal agencies the mandatory engine underneath is the RMF and SP 800-53 under FISMA, so the CSF is the communication and prioritization layer above the controls. Its Informative References map each outcome down to the controls.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners.

helper.question: How does CSF 2.0 differ from ISO/IEC 27001?
helper.answer: CSF 2.0 is an outcomes framework; ISO/IEC 27001 is a certifiable management system standard. They are complementary: an organization can hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and still use a CSF Profile to talk about outcomes, and the Informative References cross-map the two. NIST's Informative Reference Catalog lists an ISO/IEC 27001:2022 to CSF 2.0 reference.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners. The catalog sentence rests on NIST's Informative References page, read on 29 September 2026 (https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework/informative-references), which lists ISO/IEC-27001:2022-to-CSFv2.0 (1.0.0) in the catalog and says NIST does not conduct correctness testing on non-NIST submitted mappings.

helper.question: What do we do first?
helper.answer: If a mandate binds you, your trailhead's first step names it, and the trailhead's later steps supply the target. In CSF 2.0 terms: scope the Profile and gather what you need, then start with the Govern outcomes: organizational context, risk strategy, and roles. Build a Current Profile and a Target Profile, analyze the gaps and plan, then implement and update. The action plan comes from the gap between the two Profiles.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners.

helper.question: How does CSF 2.0 relate to zero trust?
helper.answer: SP 800-207 defines zero trust, and the zero trust models supply the pillars and the maturity ladder. CSF 2.0 does not define zero trust; it gives you the outcome language. Put your model's pillars as columns and the six functions as rows, fill the matrix, and the result is a zero trust Target Profile: leadership reads it in outcome language, and the Informative References under the Subcategories of each cell's Categories carry it down to SP 800-53 or your own control catalog. It also puts zero trust in Govern, Identify, and Detect, not only in Protect. Maturity stays with the zero trust model you use; CSF 2.0 Tiers characterize the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management practices.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners.

helper.question: Where are the mappings?
helper.answer: On the NIST site: the CSF 2.0 Reference Tool and the Informative Reference Catalog map each Subcategory to SP 800-53 and other sources. For either pillar model, each matrix cell carries CSF 2.0 categories; the Subcategories under those categories carry the Informative References to SP 800-53; the CISA model prints no control mapping of its own. For the {{dow}} pillars, the DoD Zero Trust Overlays map each capability to SP 800-53 controls; they are not posted publicly in 2026, so a {{dow}} component asks its own leadership or the zero trust portfolio office for the current copy, and anyone borrowing the pillars works from the capability list and the catalog. NIST's practice guide on implementing a zero trust architecture, SP 1800-35 (final, June 2025), also publishes mappings of zero trust architecture principles and technologies to commonly used security standards and guidelines; they map its example builds, not the CISA or {{dow}} pillar models.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners.

helper.question: Where do SP 800-171, CMMC, FedRAMP, ISO/IEC 27001, CIS Controls, STIGs, IL4 through IL6, and MITRE ATT&CK land?
helper.answer: SP 800-171 and CMMC are the contractor trailhead: a requirements baseline and the assessment that proves it, layers 4 and 5. FedRAMP is the governmentwide program that certifies cloud services for agency use, so it is verification (layer 5); its Rev5 path assesses an SP 800-53 baseline (layer 4), and its 20x path, widely available since June 2026, assesses Key Security Indicators instead. ISO/IEC 27001 sits beside CSF 2.0 as a management system standard. CIS Controls are a control catalog, layer 4. STIGs and SRGs are the {{dow}} configuration baseline at layer 4. IL4 through IL6 are {{dow}} cloud impact levels that set the baseline and the authorization bar, layers 4 and 5 again. ATT&CK is not a layer: it is the map of adversary behavior the stack defends against, most useful under Detect and Respond, and CORA scores against its tactics.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis from the cited entries; the answer restates none of their one-liners. The FedRAMP sentence also rests on FedRAMP's own pages, read on 29 September 2026: its post of 25 June 2026 launching the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (https://www.fedramp.gov/2026-06-25-propelling-change-fedramp-launches-consolidated-rules-for-2026/) says 20x is now a widely available FedRAMP Certification path and that from 11 June 2027 FedRAMP will no longer accept applications for new Rev5 Certifications, and the 20x certification rules (https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/20x/rules/fedramp-certification/) are stated against Key Security Indicators. A helper record carries no recheck date, so the recheck of 11 June 2027 sits on the FedRAMP glossary entry.

helper.question: Where do validated solutions and enterprise services land?
helper.answer: They are not frameworks. A solution such as Thunderdome or Flank Speed is an implementation vehicle measured against the layer 3 activities: an assessment tests which of the {{dow}} zero trust activities the service delivers. An organization that adopts one may inherit some of those activities, not all of them (inherit is this app's word: the {{dow}} activities table splits each activity between enterprise and component responsibility instead), and the way to say which are inherited and which are its own is an activity-level instrument: a record, activity by activity, of what the solution delivers and what the organization still does.

verification.note: Owner's synthesis. Inherit is the app's word: no CIO page checked on 16 September 2026 uses it for zero trust activities; the activities table splits each activity between enterprise and component responsibility instead.

helper.question: Where does operational technology land, and where does IEC 62443 fit?
helper.answer: Operational technology (OT) lands at layer 3. On the {{dow}} side it has its own baseline: activities and outcomes that adapt the enterprise zero trust activities to OT and control systems under the same seven pillars, stay aligned with the enterprise IT activities, and are implemented in addition to existing cybersecurity requirements; the document says separate guidance will be developed for weapon systems and defense critical infrastructure. Civilian agencies have no separate OT baseline on this stack: the CISA maturity model is still their model, CISA's 2026 companion, Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology, applies it to OT, and NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3 is NIST's guide to OT security. IEC 62443, from the International Electrotechnical Commission, is a series of standards for the security of industrial automation and control systems, not a zero trust model: the {{dow}} document names it, with the Purdue Model, among the established reference architectures it treats as authoritative for classifying OT systems.

ai.note: Zero trust for agents is layers 2 and 3 applied to a new subject: an agent is a non-person entity, which SP 800-207 and the user pillar already cover. The AI RMF is the outcome layer for AI risk; the Cyber AI Profile applies the six functions to AI across its three focus areas; the AI Defense Matrix covers securing AI systems, the Profile's first focus area, not AI-enabled defense. CoSAI applies SP 800-207's policy decision point to agents: authorization stays outside the model, and each tool call gets its own access decision. The SOC Profile is a worked example of one Target Profile for an AI-enabled security operations center, one outcome per function. AI as the defender's tool lands in the automation pillar, where the {{dow}} model names it and the CISA model leaves it out. None of the four frameworks in this column, nor the quick-start guide beside them, binds anyone by its own force; the instrument that governs federal agencies' use of AI, OMB Memorandum M-25-21 of 3 April 2025, is listed here as governance outside the cybersecurity stack, and it names none of them.

privacy.title: Lensatic privacy policy
privacy.description: How Lensatic handles data: it runs on your device, makes no network requests, has no account and collects nothing.
paragraphs: Lensatic runs entirely on your device. The app and the web page carry all of their content with them. Once open, the web page needs no connection, and a saved copy works offline.
Lensatic makes no network requests. Once the web page is open it loads no scripts, fonts, images or data from anywhere, and the app does not connect to the internet.
There is no account and nothing to sign in to.

Lensatic collects no personal data, usage data, identifiers or diagnostics, and stores or transmits none. The one thing the web page keeps is your theme choice (system, light or dark), saved in your browser's local storage on your device and never sent anywhere; the app keeps nothing and follows your device's light or dark setting.
Lensatic holds nothing about you, so there is nothing to retain or delete. Clearing this site's data in your browser removes the saved theme choice.
There are no third-party software development kits (SDKs), no analytics and no advertising.

In the web page and the app, the only outside links go to the public documents cited in Sources and to the source repository on GitHub; both also link to this policy and the support page. They open in your browser, under those sites' own privacy policies. This page and the support page also link to GitHub.

The web copy at https://kensden.github.io/lensatic/ is hosted by GitHub Pages. GitHub's documentation for GitHub Pages says it logs and stores the internet protocol (IP) address of each visitor for security purposes (https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/what-is-github-pages#data-collection); see also the GitHub Privacy Statement (https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement). Lensatic itself collects nothing from those visits.

Questions about this policy: open an issue on the repository's GitHub issues page, https://github.com/kensden/lensatic/issues. Opening an issue needs a GitHub account, and issues are public. An issue you open stays on GitHub under GitHub's privacy statement; ask in the issue and it will be deleted.
The effective date is the date of the content release that built this page, so it moves with each release.

support.title: Lensatic support
support.description: How to report a content error in Lensatic, how its content is re-verified, and the current content version.
paragraphs: Lensatic is an explainer of the United States federal cybersecurity framework stack. It sorts the frameworks by the question each one answers, says who each one binds, and shows where zero trust and AI land.

To report a content error, open an issue at https://github.com/kensden/lensatic/issues. Name the framework or entry, say what is wrong, and cite the primary source: the publisher's own page or document that shows the correct fact.
To ask about reusing Lensatic's code or text, open an issue on the same page.
The iOS app is built from the same content as this site. Questions and problems with the app go to the same issues page. Opening an issue needs a GitHub account, and issues are public.

Every verified entry shows the date its publisher's page was last read, and every other entry shows its status instead. An entry with a recheck date is read again when that date comes up, and no content release goes out while a recheck is overdue. The next dated recheck, if one is scheduled, is shown below.
